title: Materialization & Temp Tables
objective: After this lesson you will be able to predict when the planner inlines vs materializes CTEs, force materialization deliberately (PostgreSQL MATERIALIZED, temp tables), and stage expensive pipelines so repeated references compute once.
why: Intermediate Ch.2 warned that CTEs promise no caching — here is the other half of that truth: referenced three times, a CTE can execute three times, turning an elegant pipeline into a triple-paid bill. Knowing when the planner shares work versus repeats it, and how to force the sharing, separates queries that look fast from queries that are fast.

blocks.text: By default the planner **inlines** CTEs: it pastes each CTE's definition into every referencing spot and optimizes the whole. Inlining is usually brilliant — outer filters push inside, unused columns vanish. But inlining a CTE referenced three times means three evaluations. Elegant text, triple execution: the cost is invisible in the query and painfully visible in runtime.

blocks.code:
-- Elegant, triple-paid: heavy CTE referenced 3x (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
-- WITH heavy AS (SELECT … expensive aggregation …)
-- SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM heavy),
--        (SELECT AVG(x) FROM heavy),
--        (SELECT MAX(y) FROM heavy);
blocks.caption: Three references, potentially three full evaluations

blocks.text: Forcing the share: MATERIALIZED and temp tables

PostgreSQL lets you command it: `WITH w AS MATERIALIZED (…)` computes once into a temporary store; `NOT MATERIALIZED` forces inlining (useful when you *want* pushdown). SQLite historically materializes more aggressively — version-dependent, so verify with EXPLAIN rather than assuming. For the heaviest stages, **temp tables** (`CREATE TEMP TABLE … AS SELECT`) make staging explicit, inspectable, and indexable.

blocks.caption: Command sharing: MATERIALIZED hint or explicit temp staging

blocks.text: Temp tables are also debugging superpowers: each stage is a real table you can SELECT, count, and eyeball — the pipeline-debugging of Intermediate Ch.2 made persistent. Costs: session-scoped storage, manual cleanup discipline, and statistics the planner may lack (ANALYZE temp tables that drive big downstream joins).
When to stage: the decision rule

Stage when a CTE is (a) expensive, (b) referenced more than once, or (c) worth inspecting mid-pipeline. Don't stage cheap single-use CTEs — inlining optimizes them better than you can, and temp-table ceremony adds failure modes (stale data, forgotten drops, name collisions in shared sessions). Default inline; materialize on measured evidence (EXPLAIN showing repeated evaluation, or runtime that scales with reference count).

blocks.title: Stale-stage hazard
blocks.text: Temp tables snapshot data at creation: concurrent writers move on while your stage freezes. Short-lived staging inside one analysis is safe; long-lived temp tables feeding decisions are a staleness bug. Timestamp your stages (created_at column) so staleness is visible, not silent.

blocks.query: SELECT developer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM enrollments GROUP BY developer_id ORDER BY n DESC;
blocks.note: Run this per-developer aggregation in the sandbox — it is the 'heavy stage' shape this lesson stages. Ask: referenced once (inline it) or three times (materialize it)? The answer is always about reference count, never about elegance.

items: Inlining is the default: great for single-use CTEs (pushdown, pruning), triple-billing for 3x-referenced ones
PostgreSQL MATERIALIZED/NOT MATERIALIZED commands the choice; SQLite behavior is version-dependent — verify
Temp tables make staging explicit, inspectable, indexable — with cleanup and staleness discipline
Stage on evidence (repeated evaluation in EXPLAIN/runtime), never on elegance

exercise.prompt: A report references the per-course engagement CTE three times (averages, maxima, and a leaderboard). (a) In the sandbox, run the flat engagement aggregation and record timing feel + row counts. (b) For real PostgreSQL, write both the MATERIALIZED CTE version and the temp-table version with an index; state which you would ship and why. (c) Name the staleness guard you would add to the temp table.
hints: Sandbox aggregation: per-course COUNT + conditional completed counts (flat, GROUP BY) — the stage everything else references.
MATERIALIZED version: WITH eng AS MATERIALIZED (…) then three references. Temp version: CREATE TEMP TABLE eng AS … + CREATE INDEX + three consumers + DROP. Compare ceremony vs control.

Ship the temp table for debuggability + indexing when the stage is heavy and joined; MATERIALIZED when the win is pure recompute-avoidance. Staleness guard: created_at timestamp column checked by consumers.
exercise.why: The exercise makes the reference-count rule concrete: one stage, three consumers, two mechanisms, one shipped with reasons. Ceremony must justify itself against measured recompute — senior engineers stage deliberately, not decoratively.

quiz.q: A CTE referenced three times runs slowly although each reference is cheap. Most likely cause?
options: Repeated evaluation: inlining pastes the definition per reference — the elegant text executes up to 3x
quiz.explain: Inlining optimizes single-use stages brilliantly and multi-referenced ones expensively. Reference count, not text elegance, determines evaluation count — verify in EXPLAIN.

quiz.q: PostgreSQL WITH w AS MATERIALIZED vs NOT MATERIALIZED — when each?
options: MATERIALIZED: compute-once for multi-referenced expensive stages; NOT MATERIALIZED: force inlining when outer filters should push inside
quiz.explain: Command the trade: sharing versus pushdown/pruning. Materialize repeated heavy work; inline when outer context should optimize the inner query.

quiz.q: Temp tables beat MATERIALIZED CTEs when…
options: The stage needs inspection mid-pipeline, its own index, or reuse across statements in the session
quiz.explain: Temp tables are real, inspectable, indexable objects persisting across statements. The price is ceremony, cleanup, and staleness discipline (timestamp stages).

quiz.q: Long-lived temp table feeds a daily decision. Biggest risk?
options: Staleness: snapshot frozen at creation while writers move on — timestamp stages so age is visible
quiz.explain: Staging snapshots time. Short-lived analysis stages are safe; decision-feeding stages need visible timestamps and refresh contracts, or silent staleness corrupts choices.

summary: Inlining for single use, materialization for repeated expense — commanded in PG, verified everywhere, staged explicitly with temp tables when inspection or indexing pays. Reference count rules; elegance doesn't.
